topics: find n, p, q from first three terms

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: The first three terms, in ascending powers of x, in the expansion of \((3+px)^n\) are \(243 + 810x + qx^2\). Find the values of n, p and q.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Find the term independent of y in the expansion of \(\left(2y - \dfrac{1}{3y^2}\right)^6\). Give your answer in exact form.

questions.statement:
(a) The first three terms, in ascending powers of \(x\), in the expansion of \((3+px)^n\) are \(\;243 + 810x + qx^2\), where \(n\), \(p\) and \(q\) are constants. Find the values of \(n\), \(p\) and \(q\). [5]

(b) Find the term independent of \(y\) in the expansion of \(\;\left(2y - \dfrac{1}{3y^2}\right)^6\). Give your answer in exact form. [2]
tips: (a) The constant term is \(3^n\): \(3^n = 243 = 3^5\) gives \(n=5\) instantly. Always start with the term that has no unknown mixed in.
(a) Second term: \({}^5C_1\,3^4\,p = 810 \Rightarrow 5\times81\,p = 810 \Rightarrow p = 2\). Third: \({}^5C_2\,3^3\,p^2 = q\).
(b) General term: \({}^6C_r (2y)^{6-r}\left(-\tfrac{1}{3y^2}\right)^r\). Power of y: \((6-r) - 2r = 6-3r\); set \(=0 \Rightarrow r = 2\).
Keep the minus sign inside the bracket when you raise it to the power \(r\) — with \(r=2\) it squares away, but with odd \(r\) it survives.
markScheme: (a) B1 — \(n = 5\); M1 — considers the second term \(5\times3^4 p = 810\) (allow their n); A1 — \(p = 2\); M1 — considers the third term \(10\times3^3\times p^2 = q\); A1 — \(q = 1080\)
(b) M1 — identifies the correct term \({}^6C_2(2y)^4\left(-\frac{1}{3y^2}\right)^2\) (condone bracket/coefficient slips; may be implied by a correct answer)
(b) A1 — \(\frac{80}{3}\) oe — must be exact (allow \(\frac{240}{9}\) or \(26\tfrac23\))

questions.statement:
In the binomial expansion of \(\;\left(2+\dfrac{x}{2}\right)^n\), the first three terms in increasing powers of \(x\) are \(\;b + abx + \dfrac98 abx^2\).

Find the values of the constants \(n\), \(a\) and \(b\). [8]
tips: Write the three actual terms first: \(2^n\), \({}^nC_1 2^{n-1}\left(\tfrac{x}{2}\right)\), \({}^nC_2 2^{n-2}\left(\tfrac{x}{2}\right)^2\), then match them one at a time.
The unknowns are tangled (\(ab\) appears twice), so use RATIOS: \(\dfrac{\text{3rd}}{\text{2nd}} = \dfrac{\frac98 ab}{ab} = \dfrac98\) — the \(a\) and \(b\) cancel and only \(n\) survives.
That ratio gives \(\dfrac{n-1}{8} = \dfrac98\), so \(n = 10\). Then \(b = 2^{10}\) and \(a\) from the second term.
Ratio of consecutive binomial terms is the standard trick whenever coefficients are related but unknown.
solution: Divide the third by the second: \(\dfrac98 = \dfrac{n(n-1)2^{n-5}}{n\,2^{n-2}} = \dfrac{n-1}{8} \Rightarrow n - 1 = 9 \Rightarrow n = 10\).
markScheme: B1 — correct unsimplified second term \({}^nC_1 2^{n-1}\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)\) soi
B1 — correct unsimplified third term \({}^nC_2 2^{n-2}\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)^2\) soi
M1 — equates the ratio of their 3rd and 2nd terms to \(\frac98\) (eliminating a and b)
M1 — uses their n and b in \(ab = n2^{n-2}\);  A1 — \(a = 2.5\) oe
(⚠ The published mark scheme PDF for 4037/22 May/June 2024 ends at Q10 — this allocation is reconstructed; the answers are verified by direct substitution.)

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Using an appropriate quadratic factorisation, find the first three terms in the binomial expansion of \((9x^2+12x+4)^5\), in ascending powers of x. You must simplify your coefficients.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Find the term independent of x in the expansion of \(\left(\dfrac{6}{x^2} + \dfrac{x^4}{2}\right)^{12}\).

questions.statement:
(a) Using an appropriate quadratic factorisation, find the first three terms in the binomial expansion of \(\;(9x^2+12x+4)^5\), in ascending powers of \(x\). You must simplify your coefficients. [4]

(b) Find the term independent of \(x\) in the expansion of \(\;\left(\dfrac{6}{x^2} + \dfrac{x^4}{2}\right)^{12}\). [2]
tips: (a) "Appropriate quadratic factorisation" is the whole hint: \(9x^2+12x+4 = (3x+2)^2\), so the expression is \((3x+2)^{10}\) — a normal binomial.
(a) "Ascending powers" means start from the constant: \(2^{10} + {}^{10}C_1 2^9(3x) + {}^{10}C_2 2^8(3x)^2\). Simplify each coefficient fully.
(b) General term: \({}^{12}C_r\left(\tfrac{6}{x^2}\right)^{12-r}\left(\tfrac{x^4}{2}\right)^r\). Power of x: \(-2(12-r) + 4r = 6r - 24\); zero at \(r = 4\).
Compute carefully: the numbers get large — \({}^{12}C_4\times\dfrac{6^8}{2^4}\).
markScheme: (b) M1 — identifies \(r = 4\) or the correct term \({}^{12}C_4\left(\frac{6}{x^2}\right)^8\left(\frac{x^4}{2}\right)^4\); A1 — 51 963 120

questions.statement: Find the exact value of the term independent of \(x\) in the expansion of \(\;\left(2 + \dfrac{3}{x^2}\right)^{10}(1-4x^2)^2\). [6]
tips: A PRODUCT of two brackets: expand the small one fully — \((1-4x^2)^2 = 1 - 8x^2 + 16x^4\) — then decide which terms of the big expansion each piece needs.
You need the constant overall, so pair: (constant of big) × 1, (\(x^{-2}\) term of big) × \(-8x^2\), (\(x^{-4}\) term of big) × \(16x^4\).
From \(\left(2+\tfrac{3}{x^2}\right)^{10}\): the \(x^{-2k}\) term is \({}^{10}C_k 2^{10-k}\left(\tfrac{3}{x^2}\right)^k\) — you need \(k = 0, 1, 2\).
"Exact value" → keep it as an integer, no rounding. Three products, then add.
markScheme: B3 — \(2^{10} + 10\times2^9\times\frac{3}{x^2} + 45\times2^8\times\left(\frac{3}{x^2}\right)^2\) oe soi AND \(1-8x^2+16x^4\) soi (B2 for the first expansion correct; B1 for two correct terms in it; B1 for \(1-8x^2+16x^4\))
M2 — \(2^{10} + their\,15360\times their(-8) + their\,103680\times their\,16\) (M1 FT for any two correct terms in this sum)

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Find, in descending powers of x, the first 3 terms in the expansion of \(\left(x + \dfrac{2}{x^2}\right)^{10}\). Simplify each term as far as possible.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Find the term independent of x in the expansion of \(\left(4x^2 + \dfrac{1}{2x^2}\right)^{8}\).

questions.statement:
(a) Find, in descending powers of \(x\), the first 3 terms in the expansion of \(\;\left(x + \dfrac{2}{x^2}\right)^{10}\). Simplify each term as far as possible. [3]

(b) Find the term independent of \(x\) in the expansion of \(\;\left(4x^2 + \dfrac{1}{2x^2}\right)^{8}\). [2]
tips: (a) "Descending powers" → start with the highest power: \(x^{10}\), then let the \(\tfrac{2}{x^2}\) part in one factor at a time.
Term \(r\): \({}^{10}C_r x^{10-r}\left(\tfrac{2}{x^2}\right)^r = {}^{10}C_r 2^r x^{10-3r}\). Powers go 10, 7, 4, … (dropping by 3 each time).
(b) Power of x: \(2(8-r) - 2r = 16 - 4r = 0 \Rightarrow r = 4\). Then \({}^8C_4 4^4\left(\tfrac12\right)^4\).
Notice the pattern: each term's power drops by (sum of the two exponents) — here 3 in (a) and 4 in (b). Spot that gap and you find r in one line.
markScheme: (a) B3 — \(x^{10} + 20x^7 + 180x^4\) (B1 for each correct term)
(b) M1 — \({}^8C_4(4x^2)^4\left(\frac{1}{2x^2}\right)^4\) (may be implied by working to obtain \(r=4\)); A1 — 1120 from correct working

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: In the expansion of \((x+x^2)^8\) in ascending powers of x, the 3rd and 6th terms are equal. Find the value of x.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: In the expansion of \(\left(x + \dfrac{2}{x}\right)^n\) in decreasing powers of x, the 6th term is a constant. Find the value of the positive integer n.

parts.label: (b)(ii)

questions.statement:
(a) In the expansion of \(\;(x+x^2)^8\;\) in ascending powers of \(x\), the 3rd and 6th terms are equal. Find the value of \(x\). [3]

(b) In the expansion of \(\;\left(x + \dfrac{2}{x}\right)^n\;\) in decreasing powers of \(x\), the 6th term is a constant.

(i) Find the value of the positive integer \(n\). [2]

(ii) Find the value of the 6th term. [2]
tips: Counting rule: the \((r+1)\)th term uses \(r\). So the 3rd term is \(r=2\) and the 6th term is \(r=5\) — off-by-one errors are the main danger in this question type.
(b)(i) 6th term (\(r=5\)) of \(\left(x+\tfrac2x\right)^n\): power of x is \((n-5) - 5 = n-10\); constant \(\Rightarrow n = 10\).
(b)(ii) \({}^{10}C_5\times2^5 = 252\times32\). No x's left — that's the point of "constant".
solution: (b)(i) 6th term: \({}^nC_5 x^{n-5}\left(\dfrac{2}{x}\right)^5\), power \(= n-10\). Constant \(\Rightarrow n = 10\).
markScheme: (a) B2 — \(28x^{10}\) and \(56x^{13}\) (B1 for either); A1 — \(x = \sqrt[3]{\frac{28}{56}}\) oe nfww isw
(b)(i) B1 — the correct term in any form, e.g. \({}^nC_5 x^{n-5}\left(\frac2x\right)^5\), or \(n-5=5\) soi; A1 — \(n = 10\)

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: An arithmetic progression has common difference d. The 3rd term is 10. Write down expressions for the 1st term and the 2nd term, in terms of d only.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: When each of the first 3 terms is squared, the sum of these squares is 140. There are two possible values for d. Using your answer to part (a), find the sum of the first 200 terms of the progression with the smaller value of d.

questions.statement:
An arithmetic progression has common difference \(d\). The 3rd term of this progression is 10.

(a) Write down expressions for the 1st term and the 2nd term of this progression. Give your answers in terms of \(d\) only. [2]

(b) When each of the first 3 terms is squared, the sum of these squares is 140. There are two possible values for \(d\).
Using your answer to part (a), find the sum of the first 200 terms of the progression with the smaller value of \(d\). [7]
tips: (a) Work BACKWARDS from the known 3rd term: 2nd \(= 10-d\), 1st \(= 10-2d\). Anchoring at the known term keeps everything in one variable.
(b) Sum of squares: \((10-2d)^2 + (10-d)^2 + 10^2 = 140\). Expand carefully — the \(100\)s add to 300.
You get \(5d^2 - 60d + 160 = 0 \Rightarrow d^2-12d+32 = 0 \Rightarrow d = 4\) or \(8\). "Smaller" means \(d = 4\) → then \(a = 10-2(4) = 2\).
Finish with \(S_n = \tfrac{n}{2}\{2a + (n-1)d\}\) — the formula IS given on the paper, so no need to memorise it, but do read \(n=200\) carefully.
markScheme: (a) B2 — \(10-2d\) and \(10-d\) (B1 for either, ignore labels)
(b) M1 — squares each term and forms the sum (FT their two terms from (a)); A1 — correct equation in solvable form \(5d^2-60d+160=0\) oe
(b) M1 — factorises/solves their 3-term quadratic; A1 — \(d = 8\), \(d = 4\)
(b) M1 — finds the first term when \(d = 4\): \(a = 2\) (FT \(10-2(their\,d)\)); M1 — \(\frac{200}{2}\{4+199\times4\}\) oe FT; A1 — 80 000

topics: least n for a sum threshold

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: An arithmetic progression has first term a and common difference d. The 6th term is 1.5 times the 3rd term. The sum of the first ten terms is 255. Find the values of a and d.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Using your values of a and d, find the least number of terms for the sum of this arithmetic progression to be greater than 40 000.

questions.statement:
An arithmetic progression has first term \(a\) and common difference \(d\).
The 6th term is 1.5 times the 3rd term.
The sum of the first ten terms is 255.

(a) Find the values of \(a\) and \(d\). [4]

(b) Using your values of \(a\) and \(d\), find the least number of terms for the sum of this arithmetic progression to be greater than 40 000. [4]
tips: (a) Translate each sentence into an equation: \(a+5d = 1.5(a+2d)\) and \(\tfrac{10}{2}(2a+9d) = 255\). Two equations, two unknowns.
The first simplifies beautifully: \(a+5d = 1.5a+3d \Rightarrow 2d = 0.5a \Rightarrow a = 4d\). Substitute into the second.
(b) "Least number of terms for the sum > 40 000" → form \(\tfrac{n}{2}(2a + (n-1)d) > 40\,000\), expand to a quadratic in \(n\), solve, then round UP to the next whole number.
\(3n^2 + 21n - 80\,000 > 0\) gives \(n > 159.8\), so \(n = 160\). Check: \(n=159\) gives 39 591 (too small), \(n=160\) gives 40 080 ✓ — showing both is worth doing.
solution: \(n = \dfrac{-21+\sqrt{441+960\,000}}{6} = 159.8\ldots\), so the least whole number is \(n = 160\).
markScheme: (a) M1 — solves their simultaneous equations as far as \(a = \ldots\) or \(d = \ldots\) (dep at least B1); A1 — \(a = 12\), \(d = 3\)
(b) M1 — \(\frac{n}{2}(24+3(n-1)) * 40\,000\) with their a, d (* any inequality or =); A1 — \(3n^2+21n-80\,000 * 0\) oe in solvable form
(b) M1 — solves their quadratic; A1 — \(n = 160\) nfww (SC1 after M1 A0 for 160 by trial and improvement provided BOTH \(n=159\to39\,591\) AND \(n=160\to40\,080\) shown)

questions.statement:
A geometric progression is such that the first term is 4 and the sum of the first three terms is 7.

Find the two possible values of the common ratio and find the sum to infinity for the convergent progression. [5]
tips: Write the three terms out: \(4 + 4r + 4r^2 = 7\) — quicker than using the \(S_3\) formula for only three terms.
Rearrange to \(4r^2+4r-3 = 0\) and factorise: \((2r-1)(2r+3) = 0 \Rightarrow r = \tfrac12\) or \(r = -\tfrac32\).
Only one converges: a sum to infinity needs \(|r|<1\), so \(r=-1.5\) is rejected for the last part (but it IS one of the two required ratios).
\(S_\infty = \dfrac{a}{1-r} = \dfrac{4}{1-0.5} = 8\). The word "only" in the mark scheme means: don't also quote a value for the divergent one.
markScheme: M1 — solves or factorises their 3-term quadratic, e.g. \((2r-1)(2r+3)[=0]\)
A1 — \(\left[\frac{4}{1-0.5}=\right]\) 8 only, nfww

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: A geometric progression has a 4th term of \(\dfrac{8k^6}{27}\) and a 6th term of \(\dfrac{32k^{10}}{243}\), where k is a constant. The common ratio is positive. Find the common ratio in terms of k and the value of the first term.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Given that this geometric progression has a sum to infinity of 3, find the possible values of k.

questions.statement:
A geometric progression has a 4th term of \(\dfrac{8k^6}{27}\) and a 6th term of \(\dfrac{32k^{10}}{243}\), where \(k\) is a constant. The common ratio of this geometric progression is positive.

(a) Find the common ratio in terms of \(k\) and the value of the first term of this geometric progression. [4]

(b) Given that this geometric progression has a sum to infinity of 3, find the possible values of \(k\). [3]
tips: Terms two apart → dividing gives \(r^2\) directly: \(\dfrac{ar^5}{ar^3} = r^2 = \dfrac{32k^{10}/243}{8k^6/27}\).

Simplify the fraction of fractions: \(\dfrac{32}{243}\times\dfrac{27}{8} = \dfrac{4}{9}\), and \(k^{10}/k^6 = k^4\). So \(r^2 = \tfrac49 k^4 \Rightarrow r = \tfrac23 k^2\) (positive root — the question says so).
Then get \(a\) from \(ar^3 = \tfrac{8k^6}{27}\): the \(k\)'s cancel completely and \(a = 1\) — a nice check that you're right.
(b) \(\dfrac{1}{1-\frac23k^2} = 3 \Rightarrow 1-\tfrac23k^2 = \tfrac13 \Rightarrow k^2 = 1 \Rightarrow k = \pm1\). Both are valid: \(r = \tfrac23\) either way, and \(|r|<1\) ✓
markScheme: (a) B1 — \(ar^3 = \frac{8k^6}{27}\), \(ar^5 = \frac{32k^{10}}{243}\) soi (may be implied by a correct 5th term \(\frac{16k^8}{81}\))
(a) M1 — solves their equations to obtain \(r = mk^2\) or \(a = c\) (e.g. uses \(r^2 = \frac{\text{6th}}{\text{4th}}\)); A1 — \(r = \frac{2k^2}{3}\); A1 — \(a = 1\)
(b) B1 — uses the sum-to-infinity formula with their numeric a and their r in terms of \(k^2\)
(b) B2 — \(k = \pm1\) (B1 for each; must be from correct work)

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: A geometric progression has first term a and common ratio r, where r > 0. The sum of the 2nd and 3rd terms is 168. The sum of the 4th and 5th terms is 94.5. Find the 6th term of the progression.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Find the sum to infinity of the progression.

questions.statement:
A geometric progression has first term \(a\) and common ratio \(r\), where \(r > 0\).
The sum of the 2nd and 3rd terms of the progression is 168.
The sum of the 4th and 5th terms of the progression is 94.5.

(a) Find the 6th term of the progression. [7]

(b) Find the sum to infinity of the progression. [1]
tips: Write both facts algebraically: \(ar + ar^2 = 168\) and \(ar^3 + ar^4 = 94.5\).
Factorise each side before dividing: \(ar(1+r) = 168\) and \(ar^3(1+r) = 94.5\). Dividing kills both \(a\) AND \((1+r)\), leaving \(r^2 = \dfrac{94.5}{168}\).
\(r^2 = 0.5625 \Rightarrow r = 0.75\) (positive only, as stated). Then \(a\) from \(ar(1+r)=168\): \(a(0.75)(1.75) = 168 \Rightarrow a = 128\).
6th term \(= ar^5\) — keep it exact: \(128\times(0.75)^5 = \dfrac{243}{8}\).
markScheme: (a) M1 — correct equation where a can be directly eliminated: \(\frac{ar^3(1+r)}{ar(1+r)} = \frac{94.5}{168}\) oe
(a) M1 — \(\frac34 a + \frac{9}{16}a = 168\) oe FT their r; A1 — \(a = 128\)
(a) B1 — \(u_6 = \frac{243}{8}\) only oe isw

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: A geometric progression has 2nd term \(11x-1\), 3rd term \(x+5\) and 4th term \(x-1\). Given that \(x>0\), find the common ratio and first term of the progression.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: The sum to infinity of this progression is \(\dfrac{k}{3}\) where k is an integer. Find the value of k.

questions.statement:
It is given that a geometric progression has the following terms.

2nd term \(\;11x-1\)
3rd term \(\;x+5\)
4th term \(\;x-1\)

(a) Given that \(x > 0\), find the common ratio and first term of the progression. [6]

(b) The sum to infinity of this progression is \(\dfrac{k}{3}\), where \(k\) is an integer. Find the value of \(k\). [2]
tips: The key property: in a GP consecutive ratios are equal — \(\dfrac{\text{3rd}}{\text{2nd}} = \dfrac{\text{4th}}{\text{3rd}}\). (Equivalently \((\text{3rd})^2 = \text{2nd}\times\text{4th}\).)
Cross-multiply: \((x+5)^2 = (11x-1)(x-1)\). Expand both sides fully before collecting.
You get \(10x^2 - 22x - 24 = 0\), i.e. \(5x^2-11x-12 = 0 \Rightarrow (5x+4)(x-3) = 0\). Since \(x>0\), take \(x = 3\) — the condition exists to kill \(x=-\tfrac45\).
Then terms are 32, 8, 2 → \(r = \tfrac14\), and the first term is \(\dfrac{\text{2nd}}{r} = 32\times4 = 128\).
markScheme: (a) M1 — \(\frac{x+5}{11x-1} = \frac{x-1}{x+5}\) oe (or the r-based alternative)
(a) M1 dep — expansion, allow one error: \(x^2+10x+25 = 11x^2-12x+1\); A1 — \(10x^2-22x-24[=0]\) oe
(a) M1 dep — solves their quadratic; A1 — \(x = 3\) only nfww
(a) A1 — \(r = \frac14\) and \(a = 128\) (both)
(b) M1 — \(\frac{128}{1-0.25}\) (dep on an M in (a); FT their numeric a and r provided \(|r|<1\)); A1 — 512

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: A geometric progression has common ratio r and first term a, where a ≠ 0. The 4th term is −8 times the 7th term. Find the value of r.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: The sum of the first 5 terms of this progression is \(\dfrac{99}{32}\). Find the value of a.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: The first three terms of a different geometric progression are \(\cos\theta\sin\theta\), \(\cos\theta\sin^3\theta\) and \(\cos\theta\sin^5\theta\), for \(0<\theta<\frac{\pi}{2}\). Show that the sum to infinity of this progression is \(\tan\theta\).

questions.statement:
(a) A geometric progression has common ratio \(r\) and first term \(a\), where \(a \neq 0\). The 4th term is \(-8\) times the 7th term.

(i) Find the value of \(r\). [2]

(ii) The sum of the first 5 terms of this progression is \(\dfrac{99}{32}\). Find the value of \(a\). [2]

(b) The first three terms of a different geometric progression are \(\;\cos\theta\sin\theta,\;\cos\theta\sin^3\theta\;\) and \(\;\cos\theta\sin^5\theta\), for \(0<\theta<\dfrac{\pi}{2}\).

Show that the sum to infinity of this progression is \(\tan\theta\). [4]
tips: (a)(i) \(ar^3 = -8ar^6\). Divide by \(ar^3\) (valid: \(a\neq0\)): \(1 = -8r^3 \Rightarrow r^3 = -\tfrac18 \Rightarrow r = -\tfrac12\). Cube roots keep their sign.
(a)(ii) Use \(S_5 = \dfrac{a(1-r^5)}{1-r}\) with \(r=-\tfrac12\); take care with \((-\tfrac12)^5 = -\tfrac1{32}\) and \(1-(-\tfrac12) = \tfrac32\).
(b) Find \(r\) by dividing consecutive terms: \(\dfrac{\cos\theta\sin^3\theta}{\cos\theta\sin\theta} = \sin^2\theta\). Note \(0<\sin^2\theta<1\) on the given interval, so it converges.

(b) Then \(S_\infty = \dfrac{\cos\theta\sin\theta}{1-\sin^2\theta}\) and use the identity \(1-\sin^2\theta = \cos^2\theta\) — one \(\cos\theta\) cancels leaving \(\tfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \tan\theta\). Show every step; "show that" marks are for the chain.
solution: (b) \(r = \dfrac{\cos\theta\sin^3\theta}{\cos\theta\sin\theta} = \sin^2\theta\) (and \(0<\sin^2\theta<1\) here, so the sum to infinity exists).
markScheme: (a)(ii) M1 — \(\frac{99}{32} = a\frac{1-(-\frac12)^5}{1-(-\frac12)}\) (FT their r; must see correct substitution); A1 — \(a = \frac92\) oe
(b) B1 — \(r = \sin^2\theta\) soi nfww; B1 dep — \(\frac{\cos\theta\sin\theta}{1-\sin^2\theta}\)
(b) B1 dep — \(\frac{\cos\theta\sin\theta}{\cos^2\theta}\); B1 dep — \(\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \tan\theta\) (mark withheld for persistent omission of θ)

questions.statement:
(b) The first 3 terms of a geometric progression are \(\;\ln 2y,\;\ln 4y^2,\;\ln 16y^4\).

(i) Find the \(n\)th term of this geometric progression. [2]

(ii) Find the sum to \(n\) terms of this geometric progression, giving your answer in its simplest form. [2]

(c) The first 3 terms of a different geometric progression are \(\;\left(2w-\dfrac14\right),\;\left(2w-\dfrac14\right)^2,\;\left(2w-\dfrac14\right)^3\).

Find the values of \(w\) for which this geometric progression has a sum to infinity. [3]
tips: (b) Use log laws to reveal the pattern: \(\ln 4y^2 = \ln(2y)^2 = 2\ln 2y\) and \(\ln 16y^4 = \ln(2y)^4 = 4\ln 2y\). So the terms are \(\ln2y,\ 2\ln2y,\ 4\ln2y\) — a GP with \(r = 2\) (a NUMBER, not a log).
(b)(ii) \(S_n = \ln2y\dfrac{1-2^n}{1-2} = (2^n-1)\ln 2y\). "Simplest form" means the denominator must be gone (A0 if \(1-2\) is left showing).
(c) Here the common ratio IS the bracket: \(r = 2w-\tfrac14\). Sum to infinity exists ⟺ \(|r|<1\) ⟺ \(-1 < 2w-\tfrac14 < 1\). Solve the double inequality.
markScheme: (b)(ii) M1 — correct use of the sum formula with their non-logarithmic \(r\); A1 — \((2^n-1)\ln2y\) oe (A0 if the denominator is still present) isw
(c) B1 — \(r = 2w-\frac14\) (may be seen inside the sum-to-infinity formula)
(c) B2 — \(\left|2w-\frac14\right|<1\) or \(-1<2w-\frac14<1\) seen; final \(-\frac38 < w < \frac58\) oe (\(-0.375 < w < 0.625\))

topics: ratio of two sums to infinity
questions.statement:
A geometric progression, A, has common ratio \(r\), where \(|r| < 1\). The terms of this progression are \(a_1, a_2, a_3 \ldots\)

Another geometric progression, B, has terms \(b_1, b_2, b_3 \ldots\), where

\(b_1 = a_2,\quad b_2 = a_4,\quad b_3 = a_6 \ldots\)

The sum to infinity of A is \(S_A\) and the sum to infinity of B is \(S_B\).

Find \(\dfrac{S_B}{S_A}\) in terms of \(r\). Give your answer in its simplest form. [5]
tips: B takes every SECOND term of A (starting at the 2nd), so B's ratio is \(r_B = r^2\) and B's first term is \(b_1 = a_2 = a_1 r\).
\(S_A = \dfrac{a_1}{1-r}\) and \(S_B = \dfrac{a_1 r}{1-r^2}\).
Divide: \(\dfrac{S_B}{S_A} = \dfrac{a_1 r}{1-r^2}\times\dfrac{1-r}{a_1}\) — the \(a_1\) cancels.
Simplest form needs the difference of squares: \(1-r^2 = (1-r)(1+r)\), so the \((1-r)\) cancels leaving \(\dfrac{r}{1+r}\).
solution: Progression B takes alternate terms of A: \(r_B = r^2\), first term \(b_1 = a_2 = a_1 r\).
markScheme: B1 — \(S_A = \frac{a_1}{1-r}\) soi
B1 — \(r_B = r^2\) soi
M1 — forms \(\frac{S_B}{S_A}\) (dep on the first two B marks)
A1 — \(\frac{r}{1+r}\) cao

parts.text: Suzma is training for a marathon. In the first week she runs 10 km. Then each week she runs a distance that is 10% greater than the week before. The total distance that Suzma has run by the end of n whole weeks is more than 200 km. Find the smallest possible value of n.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: A geometric progression has 1st term a and common ratio r, where a ≠ 0 and r ≠ 1. The 1st, 2nd and 3rd terms of the geometric progression are the 1st, 3rd and 7th terms of an arithmetic progression. Find the value of r.

questions.statement:
(a) Suzma is training for a marathon. In the first week she runs 10 km. Then each week she runs a distance that is 10% greater than the week before.

The total distance that Suzma has run by the end of \(n\) whole weeks is more than 200 km. Find the smallest possible value of \(n\). [4]

(b) A geometric progression has 1st term \(a\) and common ratio \(r\), where \(a\neq0\) and \(r\neq1\). The 1st, 2nd and 3rd terms of the geometric progression are the 1st, 3rd and 7th terms of an arithmetic progression.

Find the value of \(r\). [4]
tips: (a) "10% greater each week" = GP with \(r = 1.1\), \(a = 10\). Total after n weeks: \(S_n = \dfrac{10(1.1^n - 1)}{0.1}\).
(a) The 0.1 denominator makes it collapse nicely: \(100(1.1^n - 1) > 200 \Rightarrow 1.1^n > 3\).
(a) Take logs: \(n > \dfrac{\log 3}{\log 1.1} = 11.5\), so \(n = 12\) (round UP for "more than").
(b) Write the AP terms as \(A, A+2D, A+6D\) and equate them to \(a, ar, ar^2\). Two equations: \(ar - a = 2D\) and \(ar^2 - a = 6D\).

(b) Eliminate \(D\): \(\dfrac{ar^2-a}{ar-a} = 3 \Rightarrow \dfrac{(r-1)(r+1)}{r-1} = 3 \Rightarrow r+1 = 3\). (Cancelling \((r-1)\) is legal because \(r\neq1\) is given — that's why the condition is there!)
solution: (b) AP with first term \(A\), common difference \(D\): 1st \(=A\), 3rd \(=A+2D\), 7th \(=A+6D\).
So \(2D = a(r-1)\) and \(6D = a(r^2-1)\). Dividing: \(3 = \dfrac{r^2-1}{r-1} = r+1\) (valid since \(r\neq1\)).
markScheme: (a) M1 — \(n\log1.1 * \log3\) oe or \(\log_{1.1}3\) (FT provided B1 awarded for a correct sum to n terms and their 3 > 0)
(a) A1 — \(n = 12\) (dep on all previous marks)

(b) B4 — \(r = 2\) only nfww (B3 for a correct equation solvable directly for r, e.g. \(a(r^2-3r+2)[=0]\) or \(\frac{2(r+1)(r-1)}{r-1}=6\) oe; B2 for correct equations needing rearrangement; B1 each for \(ar = a+2d\) and \(ar^2 = a+6d\))

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: An arithmetic progression has first term t and common difference 1.5. The 4th, 8th and 20th terms of this arithmetic progression form the 1st, 2nd and 3rd terms of a geometric progression. Find the value of t.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Find the common ratio of the geometric progression.

questions.statement:
An arithmetic progression has first term \(t\) and common difference 1.5.
The 4th, 8th and 20th terms of this arithmetic progression form the 1st, 2nd and 3rd terms of a geometric progression.

(a) Find the value of \(t\). [5]

(b) Find the common ratio of the geometric progression. [2]
tips: GP condition = equal ratios: \(\dfrac{t+10.5}{t+4.5} = \dfrac{t+28.5}{t+10.5}\).
Cross-multiply and expand BOTH sides — the \(t^2\) terms cancel, leaving a linear equation: \(t^2+21t+110.25 = t^2+33t+128.25\).
\(-12t = 18 \Rightarrow t = -1.5\). Then the GP terms are \(3, 9, 27\) → \(r = 3\). A negative first term is fine — don't discard it.
markScheme: (a) B1 — at least two correct terms from \(t+4.5\), \(t+10.5\), \(t+28.5\) soi (condone a for t)
(a) M1 — \(r = \frac{t+10.5}{t+4.5}\) or \(r = \frac{t+28.5}{t+10.5}\) or \(r^2 = \frac{t+28.5}{t+4.5}\) oe (FT their terms of the form \(t+1.5k\))
(a) A1 — \(\frac{t+10.5}{t+4.5} = \frac{t+28.5}{t+10.5}\) oe; A1 — clears fractions and expands: \(t^2+21t+110.25 = t^2+33t+128.25\) (must be seen)
(a) A1 — \(-1.5\) oe nfww, and no other values (dep on all previous marks)
(b) 2 — 3 nfww and no other values (M1 for \(\frac{their(-1.5)+their10.5}{their(-1.5)+their4.5}\) oe; FT their t provided \(t\neq0\))
